title: When Tool-Backed Skill Retrieval Fails: Source-Style Collapse in Executable Capability Retrieval

visual_explainer.question: How can a fixed tool corpus still lose gold-capability coverage when a dense retriever is adapted to one source style?
visual_explainer.takeaway: Source-specific adaptation can collapse on independently generated query-tool slices; ToolScout uses a query-side compatibility guard to route away from an unsafe specialist and optionally repair it with matched supervision.
visual_explainer.compared_with: A fixed source-specialist checkpoint, an aggregate-trained retriever, lexical controls, and matched-source few-shot continuation.

analysis.tldr: ToolScout diagnoses source-style collapse in executable capability retrieval: a dense retriever adapted to one ToolRet slice can preserve matched-source coverage yet lose almost all gold-tool coverage on other source slices over the same registry. A TF-IDF compatibility guard can route mismatched traffic to a broader checkpoint, but the evidence is upstream retrieval coverage rather than end-to-end agent execution.
analysis.problem: Tool-using agents often retrieve a small set of tool or skill cards before planning. If the gold capability never enters that set, later reranking and reasoning cannot recover it. A fixed capability corpus does not eliminate distribution shift when query-tool pairs come from different generators or annotation conventions.
analysis.core_idea: Measure compatibility between incoming query traffic and the source slice used to adapt a specialist retriever using a TF-IDF centroid distance. Keep the specialist in a calibrated safe band; switch unsafe traffic to an aggregate-trained checkpoint; when matched supervision accumulates, continue fine-tuning the specialist on that source.
analysis.agent_loop: observe query batch/window → estimate source compatibility → use specialist if safe or broad retriever if unsafe → retrieve top-k capability cards → rerank → optionally repair specialist with matched examples
analysis.retrieval_design: The main pipeline is dense top-20 candidate generation followed by lightweight reranking. The paper also tests lexical fusion, staged query decomposition, hierarchy, skill-card rerendering, depth sweeps, and matched-source continuation to separate candidate coverage from covered-query ranking.
compared_to: query-only rewrites and a second-corpus task-family boundary
analysis.evidence: The ToolRet-1100 specialist retains 91.8% matched-source depth-20 coverage but falls to 22.3% on the 4,996-query mixture, including 0.7% on APIGen and 0% on ToolACE. Routing to the aggregate checkpoint raises mixed coverage to 86.1%, close to the fixed aggregate retriever's 85.2%. Skill-card rerendering preserves the failure and switch. Across five collapsed sources, 20 matched examples raise the coverage-weighted global top-1 proxy from 1.3% to 53.9%.
analysis.why_it_matters: Capability retrieval is an upstream admissibility gate: missing a tool removes an action, not merely a passage. The paper is an early warning that source-specific retriever tuning can make this gate brittle even when the registry is unchanged, and that deployment-time routing needs distribution evidence rather than semantic intuition alone.
limitations: The main headline is candidate coverage/top-1 proxy, not downstream tool-use success or task completion.
The fallback is a broadly supervised aggregate retriever; fixed aggregate retrieval nearly matches the routed result, limiting the demonstrated marginal value of routing.
Source style is not query wording alone: query-side and target-tool-side shifts are coupled, and the detector has only 19 source configurations.
Routing/training/maintenance and live end-to-end latency/cost are incomplete; few-shot repair assumes matched labels become available.
